extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in journalism/communication research studying media influences, agenda-setting, and survey methods
extracted.subtask_description: Operational and conceptual guidance for researching how internal and external forces influence news content (agenda building, frame building, agenda cutting), including hypothesized relationships and survey implementation details for a national Web survey of television reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda cutting modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda cutting may occur by (1) placing an item low on the news agenda; (2) removing it from the agenda once it is there; or (3) completely ignoring it by never putting it on the agenda in the first place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tripartite definition frames the concept to be developed and measured in the study; understanding these modes helps form research questions about motives, effects on coverage, and audience cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistical constraints as cause of agenda cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda cutting may occur because of logistical constraints, such as size of the news hole and reporting staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations can only report on a certain number of topics at a time, leading to elimination of others; selection may be fortuitous rather than deliberate (McCombs). Size of news hole and staff are measurable pressures linked to content outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal and external influences (hide/camouflage) as cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda cutting may occur when people within or outside the news organization 'do their best to hide or camouflage stories.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes owners/executives or outside actors (government, advertisers, PR) deliberately or indirectly suppressing stories; illustrated by examples (e.g., internal email after 9/11). This construct is investigated in detail in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' prejudices as cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda cutting may occur because of prejudices of journalists and news organizations; gatekeepers use subjective judgment including personal prejudices when deciding what stories to omit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cutting may be unintentional; connects to classic gatekeeping theory (White). Measurement should account for subjective/unconscious biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramedia influences (components)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of this study, extramedia influences consisted of pressures from advertisers, public relations practitioners, and political and governmental sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are distinct measured constructs used to predict content outcomes (agenda-building, frame-building, agenda-cutting); hypotheses test the unique contribution of each after partialing out others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational influences (components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial organizational influences included economic pressures, pressures from owners and/or executives, and the level of ownership concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These organizational measures are hypothesized to predict outcomes on news content and to possibly interact with or mediate extramedia effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-media organization influences (components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial sources of within-media organization influences were staff-size pressures and indirect and direct management pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within-media influences are modeled as mediators between extramedia/organizational influences and content outcomes; staff size is operationalized by reporters' perceptions of inadequate staffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content influence/outcome types
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources may try to (1) influence or build the media agenda (agenda building); (2) influence the angle of a story (frame building); or (3) influence coverage decisions by convincing the media not to cover a story or aspect of it (agenda cutting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study measures separate constructs for agenda-building, frame-building, and agenda-cutting to capture different modes of influence on content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesized Model of Influences on Media Content (IOMC) using SEM
rubrics_metrics.description: A structural equation model with latent constructs (ovals) measured by observed variables (rectangles), including error terms δ and ε and disturbance terms ζ to account for measurement error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SEM requires large samples; the study uses a model-building SEM approach that splits the data (exploratory first half, confirmatory second half) to avoid overfitting and to confirm model modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling frame construction (Bacon's MediaSource + station sites)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of U.S. television stations compiled from Bacon’s MediaSource was used; stations without adequate reporter listings were supplemented by consulting station Web sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain categories were omitted (Spanish-language channels, PBS, stations without news departments, specialized channels). This two-stage approach reduces coverage error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent selection criteria: general reporters only
rubrics_metrics.description: All general reporters (not those listed as specific beats like 'crime' or 'investigative') were considered; only reporters with specific email addresses (e.g., j.doe@wxyz.com, not news@wxyz.com) were eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This resembles a census of general reporters at included stations and is intended to target those likely to give candid responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for surveying reporters (respondent selection justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters were chosen because they are further removed from the business side, likely to be more candid, are transient (less likely to protect current organization), and less likely to suffer survey fatigue compared to directors/producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justification informs respondent choice for studying perceptions of influence on content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey platform and tracking (Qualtrics unique links)
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualtrics was used to implement the Web survey; each respondent received a unique link allowing tracking of responses and preventing unnecessary reminders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No access codes/passwords were required to ease access; unique links also prevent duplicate responses and allow selective reminders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-notification and personalization (Dillman-informed recruitment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A personalized mailed pre-notification letter on official letterhead was sent before the email invitation; letters included a personal address, a postscript, and a scanned signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Dillman's Tailored Design Method improves response rates; additional touches: first-class postage, offer of non-monetary incentive (executive summary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact schedule and follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Five contacts total: postal mail pre-notification; e-mail invitation; and three e-mail reminders sent over approximately three weeks; reminders sent only to non-responders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of reminders (e.g., seven days after initial email, then about one week later, then six days later) and personalization (begin emails with first name) follow best practices to boost response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of e-mail invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: E-mail invitations were scheduled on days research suggests receive higher open rates (Wednesdays, Thursdays, or Tuesdays); the official invitation was sent on a Thursday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting optimal weekdays for sending increases likelihood messages are opened and read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow alternate modes of completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants were given the option to complete the survey by mail or by telephone in addition to the Web survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering multiple modes accommodates respondent preferences and can increase total usable responses (some returned by mail or phone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted response rate (practical goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 30% targeted response rate was set for the study given sample size, constraints, and comparability with similar Pew surveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets reflect realistic expectations for large Web surveys of journalists without intensive phone follow-ups; prior literature and resource constraints inform this choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey instrument design and pretesting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Web survey consisted of 70 questions; a pretest with academics experienced in television found the survey took an average of 13 minutes and identified ambiguous wording for revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretesting is used to reduce ambiguity, check time burden, and improve instrument clarity; minor wording adjustments were made before fielding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of incentives and official branding
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients were offered a non-monetary incentive (an executive summary of findings) and the recruitment letter was printed on official UNC School of Journalism letterhead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-monetary incentives and institutional branding can improve legitimacy and response rates; 20% requesting a copy in comparable studies indicates effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRB approval and ethical procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The study, survey, and all respondent communication were approved by the Institutional Review Board at UNC-Chapel Hill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRB approval is required for ethical human-subjects research and should be documented in recruitment and consent materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and SEM model-building approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Because SEM is a large-sample technique and a model-building SEM approach was used, an adequate (larger) sample size was required; data were randomly split to use half for exploratory model-building and half to confirm modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model-building SEM requires extra sample to avoid capitalizing on chance; splitting data increases confidence in model generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse-coding market size
rubrics_metrics.description: Market size (DMA) was reverse-coded in the data so a larger DMA number corresponded with larger-market media; hypotheses and model reflect this coding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about coding decisions in analyses and hypotheses to ensure correct interpretation of directionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses on staff size pressures (H1 & H2)
rubrics_metrics.description: H1: Staff size pressures will have a positive correlation with public relations pressures. H2: Staff size pressures will have a positive correlation with overall effects/influences on content decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalizes staff-size pressure as reporters' belief that inadequate/reduced staff negatively affects coverage; used to test links with PR pressures and content influence measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market size hypotheses (H3–H6)
rubrics_metrics.description: H3: Market size will have a negative relationship with overall effects/influences on content decisions. H4: Market size will have a negative relationship with advertising influences. H5: Market size will have a positive relationship with political pressures. H6: Market size will have a negative relationship with public relations pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses reflect literature that smaller-market media may be more susceptible to advertising influences while larger markets may face more political pressures and concentrated ownership ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramedia and organizational predictor hypotheses (H7 & H8)
rubrics_metrics.description: H7: The advertiser pressures measure is the strongest extramedia predictor of outcomes/influences on news content and coverage decisions. H8: The owner/executive pressures measure is the strongest organizational predictor of outcomes/influences on news content and coverage decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These hypotheses test the relative strength of distinct extramedia and organizational sources after accounting for other components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-cutting predictor hypotheses (H9 & H10)
rubrics_metrics.description: H9: The advertiser pressures measure is the strongest extramedia predictor of instances of agenda cutting. H10: The owner/executive pressures measure is the strongest organizational predictor of instances of agenda cutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific hypotheses focus on predictors of agenda-cutting outcomes (suppression/omission) rather than agenda-building or framing.
